agents.name: Cetuximab
agents.mechanism: Blocks growth messages at the cell surface
agents.explanation: Cetuximab attaches to EGFR on the outside of cells and blocks growth messages. In bowel cancer, a validated RAS wild-type result helps identify whether this approach is suitable. In head-and-neck cancer, weekly cetuximab may be combined with radiotherapy under a separate treatment plan. Healthy skin also uses EGFR, so skin and nail effects need early care.
agents.watch: Report rash or sore nails early. Tell the nurse immediately about infusion symptoms. Eye pain, new breathing problems or severe diarrhoea need prompt advice. Blood tests check minerals during treatment and for two months afterwards.
risks: Rash, dry skin, cracks and sore nails
Infusion reaction; rare serious lung or skin effects

questions.q: How is my treatment chosen?
questions.a: Cetuximab alone is an option for RAS wild-type bowel cancer that has spread after oxaliplatin and irinotecan have failed, when irinotecan cannot be tolerated. A separate indication combines weekly cetuximab with radiotherapy for locally advanced head-and-neck cancer; the radiation team confirms suitability, including the current NCCP catalogue criteria. Your team explains the aim, alternatives and how benefit will be reviewed.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates to understand the cycle?
questions.a: No. The graph explains a general pattern. Your hospital arranges appointments; the guide and its safety information are available without entering anything.

questions.q: Will I have a pump at home?
questions.a: There is no home fluorouracil pump in this regimen. Your team chooses a cannula or central line based on your veins and wider treatment plan.

questions.q: What happens if a dose is delayed?
questions.a: The team checks the cause and may delay, reduce, change or stop one medicine. Ask which component changes and when you should next attend; do not restart yourself.

questions.q: How will I know whether it is helping?
questions.a: Scans, symptoms and clinical review assess benefit. A rash, side effect or good day alone cannot show whether the cancer is responding.

questions.q: What about radiotherapy?
questions.a: For the head-and-neck indication, cetuximab starts one week before radiation and continues weekly alongside it. The graphic below shows the relationship. Colorectal cetuximab alone does not include a routine radiation course.

questions.q: What about fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding?
questions.a: Discuss fertility preservation and reproductive plans before treatment. Ask for the contraception and breastfeeding instructions for every medicine; the whole regimen may require longer precautions than one medicine alone.

questions.q: Why is RAS testing mentioned?
questions.a: RAS testing selects cetuximab treatment in colorectal cancer. It is not the selection test for the separate head-and-neck radiotherapy indication. Confirm the cancer-specific plan with your team.

questions.q: Which checks continue when treatment changes or finishes?
questions.a: Monthly electrolytes, magnesium and calcium for two months after the last cetuximab dose; assign responsibility before treatment ends. Response assessment follows the consultant plan; head/neck radiation follow-up is coordinated separately.

patient.title: Panitumumab + modified FOLFOX-6

agents.name: Panitumumab
agents.mechanism: Blocks growth messages at the cell surface
agents.explanation: Panitumumab attaches to EGFR, a receptor on the outside of cells. This can interrupt signals that help some bowel cancers grow. A tumour RAS test helps identify whether this approach is suitable. EGFR also supports healthy skin, which explains why skin and nail changes need attention.
agents.watch: Report rash, painful cracks or nail changes early. Eye pain or blurred vision, new breathing symptoms, severe diarrhoea, or blistering skin need prompt assessment. Blood tests check minerals such as magnesium.
risks: Rash, dry skin, cracks and sore nails
Infusion reaction; rare serious lung or skin effects

agents.name: Oxaliplatin
agents.explanation: Oxaliplatin makes links within DNA. These interfere with copying and repair, which can stop a cancer cell dividing. Healthy tissues can also be affected.
agents.watch: Cold can trigger tingling or throat discomfort. Tell the team about persistent numbness, difficulty with buttons or walking, or infusion symptoms. New breathing difficulty always needs assessment.
risks: Persistent sensory neuropathy, sometimes lasting after treatment
Rare serious lung or blood complications

agents.name: Folinic acid
agents.explanation: Folinic acid helps fluorouracil remain bound to an enzyme needed to make DNA. In this regimen it increases fluorouracil activity and can also increase its unwanted effects. It is not a vitamin supplement to start yourself.
agents.watch: The combined treatment can increase mouth soreness and diarrhoea. Report these promptly. Rare allergic reactions can occur.

agents.name: Fluorouracil
agents.explanation: Fluorouracil interferes with the production and use of DNA and RNA, the instructions cells need to grow. The infusion extends exposure over approximately two days.
agents.watch: Diarrhoea, mouth sores and skin soreness may become serious. Chest pain during the pump infusion needs emergency assessment. Unexpected severe early toxicity can occur even after DPD testing.
risks: Severe early toxicity including DPD-related toxicity

questions.q: Why do I need a RAS test?
questions.a: RAS is part of the growth-signalling pathway inside cancer cells. If it is changed by a mutation, blocking EGFR is unlikely to help. Your team needs a validated wild-type RAS result before panitumumab. Other tumour tests and the treatment aim also affect the choice.

questions.q: Is this the same as checkpoint immunotherapy?
questions.a: Panitumumab is a targeted antibody against EGFR. It works differently from checkpoint treatments used in some other cancer regimens. Ask your team which treatment class and side effects apply to you.

questions.q: Does a rash mean the treatment is working?
questions.a: A rash is a recognised drug effect, but it cannot tell you whether your cancer is responding. Report it early so it can be treated. Scans, symptoms and clinical review guide the response assessment.

questions.q: Will I need radiotherapy as part of this cycle?
questions.a: These panitumumab regimens do not contain a scheduled radiotherapy course. If radiotherapy is recommended separately, your oncology teams will explain its purpose and timing. Do not assume it occurs on infusion or pump days.

questions.q: What about pregnancy, breastfeeding or fertility?
questions.a: Discuss pregnancy plans and fertility before treatment. Panitumumab requires contraception during treatment and for two months afterwards, and breastfeeding should be avoided for that period. When chemotherapy is also included, its precautions may last longer; ask for the instructions for the whole regimen.

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: Which checks continue when treatment changes or finishes?
questions.a: Monthly electrolytes, magnesium and calcium for two months after the last panitumumab dose. Assess cumulative oxaliplatin neuropathy and cold sensitivity throughout treatment and after stopping; disease scans follow the consultant plan.

patient.phases_title: Treatment, review and the next cycle
patient.phases_note: There is no fixed four-cycle course. Scans, symptoms and your priorities guide continuation or changes. With combination treatment, the antibody and chemotherapy may need different holds or changes.

patient.safety_note: There are no guaranteed safe days. Act on fever, sudden illness or a new serious symptom whenever it occurs. Do not wait for the next appointment.
patient.teachback: Can you explain which medicines you are receiving, the schedule, the contact plan and the symptoms that need prompt help?

items.text: RAS wild type is required for panitumumab. Your team also considers the cancer location, other molecular results, previous treatment and whether surgery or other local treatment could be useful. A positive eligibility result is not a promise of benefit.

chapters.title: Before you start and before each cycle
chapters.intro: The team checks that the plan remains suitable.

items.title: Checks and medicines
items.text: Review blood counts, kidney/liver function and minerals, current symptoms, allergies and all medicines. DPD testing is needed before fluorouracil unless already documented. Tell the team about severe reactions to previous chemotherapy.

items.title: Skin, eyes and breathing
items.text: Tell the team about an existing rash, skin infection, dry or painful eyes, contact lenses, or previous lung inflammation. Report new eye pain, light sensitivity or visual change promptly.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: Build the plan around what matters to you.

items.title: Skin and nails
items.text: Ask for your skin-care plan before the first infusion. Use the recommended moisturiser and sun protection; your team may prescribe a cream or an antibiotic. Do not use ordinary acne treatments without advice. Avoid friction on sore skin and tell the team about painful nail folds.

items.title: Food, activity and support
items.text: Keep fluids and nourishing food within reach. Pace activity around energy levels and ask for dietetic, emotional or practical support. If symptoms prevent eating, drinking or usual tasks, contact the team.

items.title: Pregnancy and fertility
items.text: Discuss pregnancy plans and fertility before treatment. Panitumumab requires contraception during treatment and for two months afterwards, and breastfeeding should be avoided for that period. When chemotherapy is also included, its precautions may last longer; ask for the instructions for the whole regimen.

chapters.title: When treatment changes or finishes
chapters.intro: Follow-up continues after the last infusion.

items.title: Monitoring and recovery
items.text: Continue your skin plan and planned magnesium, calcium and potassium checks for about eight weeks after panitumumab. New symptoms still need review. Ask when to stop prescribed supportive medicines.

items.title: Treatment choices
items.text: Your team may pause, reduce, change or stop one or more medicines. Ask which medicine changes, why, and what the next review will assess. Supportive and palliative care can help alongside active treatment.

chapters.title: Recognise changes early
chapters.intro: You do not need to identify the responsible medicine before asking for help.

items.title: When to call
items.text: Report new breathing difficulty, eye pain or blurred vision, blistering or infected skin, severe diarrhoea or dehydration promptly. Also report new chest pain, fever or a line/pump problem immediately.

items.title: Track impact, not just a score
items.text: Describe when symptoms began, whether they are worsening, and whether they affect food, fluids, sleep, walking or daily tasks. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Use the passport if it helps; it is not required to access this information.

items.title: Cold sensitivity and nerves
items.text: Oxaliplatin may cause cold-triggered tingling or throat sensations. Avoid cold exposure as instructed, and do not suck ice chips during fluorouracil in this regimen. New breathing difficulty still needs assessment. Persistent numbness or trouble with buttons or walking must be reported.

agents.name: Panitumumab
agents.mechanism: Blocks growth messages at the cell surface
agents.explanation: Panitumumab attaches to EGFR, a receptor on the outside of cells. This can interrupt signals that help some bowel cancers grow. A tumour RAS test helps identify whether this approach is suitable. EGFR also supports healthy skin, which explains why skin and nail changes need attention.
agents.watch: Report rash, painful cracks or nail changes early. Eye pain or blurred vision, new breathing symptoms, severe diarrhoea, or blistering skin need prompt assessment. Blood tests check minerals such as magnesium.
risks: Rash, dry skin, cracks and sore nails
Infusion reaction; rare serious lung or skin effects

agents.name: Irinotecan
agents.explanation: The body converts irinotecan into SN-38. This traps an enzyme called topoisomerase I while DNA is being copied, causing damage that can stop cancer cells dividing. Normal bowel and blood-forming cells can also be affected.
agents.watch: Tell the nurse immediately about cramps, sweating or diarrhoea during the infusion. Diarrhoea starting later needs the separate written treatment and contact plan.
risks: Rare serious lung or allergic reactions

agents.name: Folinic acid
agents.explanation: Folinic acid helps fluorouracil remain bound to an enzyme needed to make DNA. In this regimen it increases fluorouracil activity and can also increase its unwanted effects. It is not a vitamin supplement to start yourself.
agents.watch: The combined treatment can increase mouth soreness and diarrhoea. Report these promptly. Rare allergic reactions can occur.

agents.name: Fluorouracil
agents.explanation: Fluorouracil interferes with the production and use of DNA and RNA, the instructions cells need to grow. The infusion extends exposure over approximately two days.
agents.watch: Diarrhoea, mouth sores and skin soreness may become serious. Chest pain during the pump infusion needs emergency assessment. Unexpected severe early toxicity can occur even after DPD testing.
risks: Severe early toxicity including DPD-related toxicity

questions.q: Why do I need a RAS test?
questions.a: RAS is part of the growth-signalling pathway inside cancer cells. If it is changed by a mutation, blocking EGFR is unlikely to help. Your team needs a validated wild-type RAS result before panitumumab. Other tumour tests and the treatment aim also affect the choice.

questions.q: Is this the same as checkpoint immunotherapy?
questions.a: Panitumumab is a targeted antibody against EGFR. It works differently from checkpoint treatments used in some other cancer regimens. Ask your team which treatment class and side effects apply to you.

questions.q: Does a rash mean the treatment is working?
questions.a: A rash is a recognised drug effect, but it cannot tell you whether your cancer is responding. Report it early so it can be treated. Scans, symptoms and clinical review guide the response assessment.

questions.q: Will I need radiotherapy as part of this cycle?
questions.a: These panitumumab regimens do not contain a scheduled radiotherapy course. If radiotherapy is recommended separately, your oncology teams will explain its purpose and timing. Do not assume it occurs on infusion or pump days.

questions.q: What about pregnancy, breastfeeding or fertility?
questions.a: Discuss pregnancy plans and fertility before treatment. Panitumumab requires contraception during treatment and for two months afterwards, and breastfeeding should be avoided for that period. When chemotherapy is also included, its precautions may last longer; ask for the instructions for the whole regimen.

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: Which checks continue when treatment changes or finishes?
questions.a: Monthly electrolytes, magnesium and calcium for two months after the last panitumumab dose. Disease assessment follows the consultant plan. Escalate persistent diarrhoea, fever or dehydration between visits. Check INR if taking warfarin, as clinically indicated.

patient.title: Pembrolizumab + pemetrexed + carboplatin
patient.purpose: The combination aims to control metastatic non-squamous lung cancer. Your team checks cancer markers, your health and your preferences. Chemotherapy and immunotherapy work in different ways.

agents.name: Pembrolizumab
agents.explanation: PD-1 is a control switch on T cells, a type of immune cell. When it connects with PD-L1 or PD-L2, the T cell receives a signal to reduce its activity. Some cancers use this pathway to escape immune attack. Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, helping T cells recognise and attack the cancer. It does not directly poison cancer cells like chemotherapy. Releasing this brake can also allow immune cells to attack healthy organs, which explains the different side-effect pattern and why symptoms can appear after treatment stops.
agents.watch: The immune system can also inflame healthy organs. New cough, diarrhoea, unusual weakness, severe headache, thirst or a spreading rash need prompt advice. Effects can start during treatment or after it finishes.
risks: Immune inflammation of lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys, glands, skin and other organs
Effects can develop after treatment ends

agents.name: Pemetrexed
agents.explanation: Pemetrexed is an antifolate: it blocks several enzymes that cells use to turn folate-dependent materials into DNA and RNA building blocks. With fewer building blocks, cancer cells have more difficulty copying their genetic instructions and dividing. Healthy rapidly renewing tissues, including bone marrow and the mouth lining, can also be affected. That helps explain low blood counts and mouth soreness. Prescribed folic acid and vitamin B12 reduce toxicity; they are part of the treatment, not supplements to omit because the drug is an antifolate.
agents.watch: Healthy tissues can be affected too: low blood counts, a sore mouth, rash and kidney problems are important. Folic acid, vitamin B12 and prescribed steroids help reduce particular risks.
risks: Fatigue, nausea, mouth soreness and rash
Kidney toxicity; folate and B12 supplementation are required

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin is a platinum-containing chemotherapy. Inside cells, it forms chemical attachments to DNA, including links that stop DNA strands working normally. This disrupts copying and repair and can lead to cell death. Healthy cells can also be injured, especially blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. The kidneys help remove carboplatin, so kidney function is used to calculate the dose. AUC 5 describes a target drug exposure over time; it is not a fixed dose of 5 mg.
agents.watch: Low blood counts, nausea and vomiting can occur. An allergic reaction is also possible: tell the nurse immediately if you feel flushed, itchy, tight-chested or unwell during the drip.
risks: Low blood counts, infection or bleeding

questions.q: How will we know if it is helping?
questions.a: Ask your oncologist what the treatment is aiming to achieve for you, when scans are planned and what would lead to continuing, changing or stopping it. How you feel and the amount of side effects do not reliably show how well treatment is working.

questions.q: Why might a cycle be delayed?
questions.a: A delay can give time to recover or investigate a new symptom. It is a safety decision, not a personal failure. Ask which medicines are affected, what needs to improve and when you will be reviewed.

questions.q: Will I get every side effect?
questions.a: No. The body map shows selected possibilities, not a prediction. Ask about common effects, serious less common effects, and any long-term risks that matter particularly to you. The same symptom can have several causes.

questions.q: What should I organise before starting?
questions.a: Confirm blood-test and Day Ward arrangements, transport home, your medicines schedule and a thermometer. Keep the oncology contact instructions and immunotherapy alert card available. Ask for an interpreter or accessible information if useful.

questions.q: What else belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: Your priorities, expected benefit, alternatives including supportive care, fertility, contraception, pregnancy or breastfeeding, work, driving and the possibility of lasting side effects. You can ask more questions or reconsider treatment at any stage.

questions.q: Do more side effects mean the treatment is working better?
questions.a: No. Side effects are not a reliable personal measure of cancer response. Report them so they can be treated; do not tolerate serious symptoms in the hope that they are a sign of benefit.

questions.q: Will the same three medicines continue indefinitely?
questions.a: No. The planned carboplatin phase is up to four cycles. Pembrolizumab and pemetrexed may continue afterwards. Ask about the intended duration of each drug, review points and reasons for a change.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide whether my blood tests are good enough?
questions.a: No. Your treating team combines blood results, symptoms, prior toxicity and the prescribing protocol. This page explains the checks; it does not authorise a dose or a treatment decision.

questions.q: What should I say when calling about a symptom?
questions.a: Say you are receiving pembrolizumab, pemetrexed and carboplatin (or your current maintenance drugs), the last treatment date, what has changed, when it started, your temperature and whether you can eat, drink and pass urine. Say if symptoms are worsening. Do not delay calling to collect every detail.

questions.q: Which checks continue when treatment changes or finishes?
questions.a: Folic acid continues throughout pemetrexed and for 21 days after its last dose. Vitamin B12 remains due every three cycles while pemetrexed continues. Immune-related symptoms can arise during or after treatment; maintain alert-card and urgent-contact education. Response imaging follows the consultant plan.

chapters.title: Understanding your diagnosis and treatment aim
chapters.intro: Start here if the names and abbreviations are new. You can read one section at a time and return when you need it.

items.title: What do the cancer terms mean?
items.text: Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is a broad group of lung cancers. “Non-squamous” describes the cells seen by the pathologist and includes adenocarcinoma. “Metastatic” means the cancer has spread beyond its original site. “First-line” means the first drug treatment chosen for this stage of illness. A regimen is a planned combination and schedule of medicines.

items.title: What is the treatment trying to achieve?
items.text: The usual aims in this setting are to control cancer, help symptoms and extend life while preserving quality of life. It is generally not given with an expectation of cure. Some people have prolonged benefit; others do not respond. Ask what success would look like for you: easier breathing, less pain, stable scans, more time or a balance of these.

items.title: Why are tumour tests important?
items.text: The team considers the cancer’s molecular results and PD-L1 result alongside your health. EGFR and ALK alterations can point towards a different treatment approach. PD-L1 is a protein involved in immune signalling; its result helps inform choices but is not a guarantee of benefit. This combination has evidence across PD-L1 groups, including low expression. Ask whether all relevant tumour testing is complete before your plan is finalised.

items.title: What are the alternatives?
items.text: The right comparison depends on tumour tests, symptoms, fitness and your preferences. Ask whether targeted therapy, immunotherapy alone, a different chemotherapy approach, a clinical trial or symptom-focused care is relevant. Supportive and palliative care can accompany active cancer treatment: help with breathlessness, pain, appetite and family concerns is not reserved for the last days of life.

chapters.title: Before the first infusion
chapters.intro: Use this as a conversation checklist. Your own hospital’s instructions and prescription take priority.

items.title: Tell the team your starting point
items.text: Describe your usual breathing, bowel pattern, energy, skin symptoms and ability to manage daily tasks. Mention autoimmune illness, organ transplant, previous lung inflammation, infections and all regular medicines. Changes are easier to recognise when the team knows what is normal for you. Do not minimise symptoms because you are worried treatment will be delayed.

items.title: Make the first week manageable
items.text: Have the oncology and out-of-hours numbers available, a working thermometer, your medicine schedule and a way to get urgent help. Ask who to ring if you miss a supportive medicine. Plan transport and practical help if needed. Bring your questions and, if you wish, someone you trust to listen and take notes.

items.title: During the infusion visit
items.text: Expect a symptom review and checks before drugs are released. Treatment is given through a cannula or another agreed venous access device. Tell the nurse immediately about burning or swelling around the drip, itching, flushing, dizziness or breathing changes. Waiting, pharmacy preparation and observation add to the time spent receiving the medicines.

chapters.title: What your tests and scans are checking
chapters.intro: Different checks answer different questions: whether treatment is safe today, whether a symptom needs investigation, and whether the cancer is responding.

items.title: Blood counts: three separate jobs
items.text: Neutrophils help fight infection; a low level can make infection dangerous. Haemoglobin carries oxygen; a low level can contribute to tiredness and breathlessness. Platelets help stop bleeding; low levels can cause bruising or bleeding. Feeling well does not prove your counts are normal, and a previous normal result does not rule out a new problem.

items.title: Kidney, liver and hormone checks
items.text: Kidneys remove medicines and influence carboplatin dosing. Liver tests can show injury before obvious symptoms develop. Pembrolizumab can disturb hormone-producing glands, so blood glucose and thyroid monitoring matter too. Symptoms can prompt additional tests. Always report how you feel: routine blood tests alone do not exclude every immune side effect.

items.title: Scans and the treatment decision
items.text: Your team sets the scan schedule and compares scans with symptoms and examination findings. Stable disease can be a worthwhile result. New symptoms need review even before the next scan. An unusual scan pattern sometimes needs clarification; do not assume that apparent growth is simply an immune response or that feeling worse means treatment is working.

items.title: Why a delay or a change can be appropriate
items.text: A pause may allow recovery or investigation. Chemotherapy doses can sometimes be reduced. Pembrolizumab is generally held or stopped for relevant toxicity rather than dose-reduced. Ask which drug is changing and why; stopping one drug does not automatically mean stopping every part of the plan. Long-term treatment decisions belong in a discussion about benefit, risk and what matters to you.

chapters.title: Side effects: what they mean and what to do
chapters.intro: These are selected possibilities, not a prediction or a complete medicine leaflet. You do not need to work out the cause before asking for help.

items.title: Nausea, vomiting and appetite change
items.text: Medicines can stimulate sickness pathways in the gut and brain. Take preventive anti-sickness medicines as prescribed, even when you initially feel well. Smaller meals and frequent sips may be easier. Report poor control early so the plan can be adjusted. Persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down or much less urine need prompt advice. Do not wait until you are very dehydrated.

items.title: Fatigue: common, but not always “just treatment”
items.text: Fatigue may reflect treatment, disturbed sleep, reduced intake, anaemia or another illness. Balance rest with manageable movement and prioritise activities that matter to you. A sudden change, severe weakness, dizziness, breathlessness or inability to manage basic tasks needs assessment; hormone problems and other complications can resemble ordinary tiredness. Tell the team how fatigue affects daily life, not just that you feel tired.

items.title: Mouth soreness, ulcers and taste
items.text: Treatment can injure the lining of the mouth. Use a soft toothbrush, gentle mouth care and the rinses recommended by your team. Choose softer foods and avoid foods that sting. Ask for pain relief early. Report ulcers, white patches, painful swallowing or reduced intake; difficulty drinking or fever needs urgent advice. Arrange dental care with the oncology team before procedures.

items.title: Diarrhoea or abdominal pain
items.text: Pemetrexed can affect the bowel, but pembrolizumab can also cause bowel inflammation (colitis). Report new diarrhoea promptly, including how many stools above your normal pattern, blood or mucus, night-time symptoms and pain. Do not assume it is a harmless expected effect or rely on anti-diarrhoeal medicine without the team’s instructions. Severe pain, bleeding or dehydration needs urgent assessment.

items.title: Constipation
items.text: Anti-sickness drugs, opioid painkillers, less food and less movement can slow the bowel. Ask about a bowel plan if you are prone to constipation or take opioids. Keep track of your usual pattern. Increasing abdominal pain, vomiting, a swollen abdomen or inability to pass wind needs prompt assessment rather than simply increasing laxatives.

items.title: Bruising, bleeding or breathlessness
items.text: Chemotherapy may reduce platelets or red cells. Report unexpected bruises, nosebleeds, bleeding gums or increasing breathlessness. Heavy bleeding, black stools with weakness, severe chest pain or severe breathing difficulty need emergency help. Do not start iron or alter blood thinners without review: the cause and treatment need to be established.

items.title: Skin, hair, nerves and hearing
items.text: Skin can become dry, itchy or develop a rash; report new changes, especially if spreading. Hair may thin. Tingling, numbness or hearing changes should be reported before the next dose because they may affect the plan. Blisters, peeling skin or sores involving the eyes or mouth need urgent assessment. Use gentle skin care and discuss suitable sun protection.

chapters.title: Pembrolizumab: symptoms that deserve special attention
chapters.intro: Immune treatment can cause inflammation in healthy organs, during treatment or after it ends. Keep your immunotherapy alert card and tell other healthcare professionals you have received pembrolizumab.

items.title: Lungs, bowel, liver and kidneys
items.text: New cough or breathlessness, diarrhoea, yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, reduced urine or swelling can signal inflammation. These symptoms also have other causes, including infection and cancer. Contact the team promptly for assessment rather than trying to identify the organ or diagnosis yourself.

items.title: Hormones, heart and nervous system
items.text: Report unusual weakness, persistent headache, dizziness, marked thirst, frequent urination, palpitations, muscle weakness or changes in vision. Severe chest pain, collapse, confusion, seizures or major breathing difficulty require emergency care. Some hormone effects need ongoing replacement treatment even after immunotherapy stops.

items.title: Why early reporting matters
items.text: The team may pause treatment and investigate. Some reactions need steroids or other immune-suppressing treatment; others need hormone replacement. These are different from the short planned steroid course around chemotherapy. Do not start leftover steroids, change their dose or stop a prescribed course yourself. Carry the treatment name when attending emergency care.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: The aim is a plan that fits your life as well as your treatment. Bring practical concerns to the team early.

items.title: Food, fluids and weight
items.text: Aim for enough food and fluid to maintain strength, using foods you tolerate. Tell the team about weight loss, swallowing problems or difficulty shopping or cooking; ask for dietitian support. A fixed fluid target is not right for everyone, particularly with heart or kidney disease. “Anti-cancer” diets, fasting and high-dose supplements are not substitutes for treatment and can create nutritional or interaction problems.

items.title: Movement, work and rest
items.text: Try activity that feels manageable and increase or reduce it according to symptoms. Short walks or simple daily tasks may be more realistic than your usual exercise. Discuss work adjustments and travel plans. Do not drive if dizzy, unusually tired or affected by sedating medicines. Sudden deterioration should prompt assessment, not an attempt to push through exercise.

items.title: Infection precautions without isolation
items.text: Wash hands, practise food hygiene and avoid close contact with people who are unwell. Ask about vaccinations and their timing; some vaccines are unsuitable during treatment. You can usually still spend time with family. Keep your urgent contact plan available: precautions reduce risk but do not make fever or sudden illness safe to watch at home.

items.title: Intimacy, fertility and pregnancy
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment if relevant. Treatment may harm a developing baby; ask for a written contraception plan covering all three medicines and the period after the last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment; confirm when it would be safe to restart. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy. Ask about barrier protection and handling body fluids under your hospital’s advice.

items.title: Emotional support and choices
items.text: It is reasonable to feel worried, angry, uncertain or overloaded. Ask for psycho-oncology, counselling, social work or family support. You can request information in smaller pieces, an interpreter or a written summary. Tell the team what you most want to preserve in daily life. You can revisit treatment decisions and ask for more time or another explanation.

chapters.title: A short treatment dictionary
chapters.intro: Terms you may hear in clinic.

items.title: Cycle · induction · maintenance
items.text: A cycle is a planned treatment-and-interval period. Induction is the initial combination phase. Maintenance is ongoing treatment after that phase; it does not mean side-effect-free treatment.

items.title: Response · stable disease · progression
items.text: Response means the cancer has reduced by the assessment used. Stable disease means it has not changed enough to meet response or progression criteria. Progression means growth or spread meeting the assessment criteria. Your team interprets these alongside how you are feeling.

items.title: Neutropenia · anaemia · thrombocytopenia
items.text: Neutropenia means low infection-fighting neutrophils. Anaemia means low haemoglobin. Thrombocytopenia means low platelets. These are different results with different implications; one normal number does not establish that all treatment risks are low.

items.title: Immune-related · colitis · pneumonitis
items.text: Immune-related effects come from immune activity against healthy tissue. Colitis means inflammation of the colon; pneumonitis means inflammation in the lungs. A symptom alone cannot establish either diagnosis.

agents.name: Capecitabine
agents.explanation: After you swallow capecitabine, your body changes it into fluorouracil. This interferes with the DNA and RNA processes cells use to grow. Normal cells can also be affected, which helps explain mouth soreness, bowel symptoms and changes in blood counts.
agents.watch: Stop tablets and contact the team for significant diarrhoea, painful mouth ulcers, hand-foot soreness affecting activities, fever or dehydration. Chest pain needs urgent assessment. Do not restart until instructed.

agents.name: Pelvic radiotherapy
visual: Cells lose the ability to multiply
agents.explanation: Radiation is directed at the planned area. Capecitabine helps sensitise cancer cells to it. Nearby bowel, bladder and skin may also become irritated. Effects can build over the weeks and may continue after the final session.
agents.watch: Tell the radiotherapy team about diarrhoea, pain, skin soreness or urinary changes. Discuss possible longer-term bowel, bladder, sexual and fertility effects before treatment.

chapters.intro: The radiation team gives a separate, individual plan.

items.title: Before treatment
items.text: Planning appointments define the area to treat and how you will be positioned. Follow the exact bowel and bladder preparation instructions from your centre.

items.title: Daily sessions and tablets
items.text: NCCP 00586 specifies capecitabine Days 1–5 of each week. Confirm the plan if a session is missed, postponed or falls around a bank holiday; do not add weekend tablets yourself.

items.title: After the course
items.text: Side effects can accumulate and continue after treatment. Ask about follow-up and possible late bowel, bladder, sexual or fertility effects.

chapters.title: Tests and checks
chapters.intro: Monitoring helps the team decide whether treatment can continue.

items.title: DPD testing
items.text: DPD helps break down fluoropyrimidine medicines. Low activity can cause severe toxicity; testing before treatment helps guide the plan but cannot prevent every serious reaction.

items.title: Blood, kidney and liver results
items.text: Counts, kidney and liver function are checked before each cycle. Diarrhoea and poor intake can worsen kidney function and make tablets harder to tolerate.

items.title: Your symptoms matter
items.text: Report bowel frequency, stoma output, mouth soreness, hand-foot pain, chest symptoms and what daily activities you can no longer manage.

items.title: Additional checks
items.text: Radiotherapy reviews also address pelvic skin, bowel, urinary and nutritional problems.

chapters.title: Recognise symptoms and act
chapters.intro: Do not wait for the next appointment if you feel unwell.

items.title: Bowel and hydration
items.text: Report diarrhoea or increased stoma output early. Inability to drink, dizziness, very little urine, severe pain or blood in stool needs prompt assessment.

items.title: Hands, feet and mouth
items.text: Pain, cracking, peeling or ulcers that affect normal activities or eating/drinking need advice. Gentle preventive care helps, but does not replace reporting.

items.title: Chest symptoms and infection
items.text: Stop capecitabine and seek urgent assessment for chest pain. Fever, shaking chills or sudden illness needs immediate oncology contact, even if the temperature is normal.

items.title: Treatment-specific effects
items.text: Pelvic radiation can cause bowel, bladder and skin irritation, with possible later effects. Ask about sexual health and fertility before treatment.

chapters.title: Daily life and other medicines
chapters.intro: Make the plan fit your practical needs.

items.title: Eating, drinking and activity
items.text: Aim for tolerable meals and fluids; contact the team if intake falls. Gentle activity and rest can be adjusted to your energy. Ask for dietetic help if needed.

items.title: Medicine and supplement checks
items.text: Check new medicines with oncology pharmacy. Warfarin can require closer INR checks; phenytoin levels may need monitoring. Brivudine is an important prohibited interaction.

items.title: Family, work and fertility
items.text: Ask about infection exposure, work, intimacy, contraception, fertility and any caring responsibilities. Use the medicine-specific duration of precautions given by your team.

items.title: Procedures and travel
items.text: Plan transport and support around appointments. Ask which symptoms or blood-count problems affect travel and when to contact the service.

chapters.title: Review, recovery and follow-up
chapters.intro: Your plan can change as treatment progresses.

items.title: Dose changes are individual
items.text: A pause or reduction may be needed because of symptoms, blood results or kidney function. The team considers the treatment aim and other options.

items.title: After the last dose
items.text: Keep reporting new or persistent symptoms after treatment ends. Your team confirms follow-up, scans and recovery support; the timeline is not a forecast.

items.title: Prepare for review
items.text: Bring questions, symptoms and missed-dose records. Tell the team what matters most to you and ask them to explain the next decision.

questions.q: What is the aim of my treatment?
questions.a: Capecitabine tablets are given with pelvic radiotherapy for locally advanced rectal cancer. The tablets help the radiation treatment work; your team confirms how this fits with surgery and other treatment.

questions.q: Which days do I take the tablets?
questions.a: Capecitabine twice daily on Days 1–5 of each 7-day cycle, alongside radiotherapy, for up to 5–6 cycles. Follow the written plan for treatment days and interruptions.

questions.q: What if I forget a dose or vomit?
questions.a: Do not take an extra dose. Take the next planned dose at its usual time unless treatment has been stopped; report repeated vomiting and check with the team if unsure.

questions.q: When should I stop tablets and call?
questions.a: Stop capecitabine and contact oncology for significant diarrhoea, painful mouth or hand-foot symptoms affecting activity, vomiting that prevents drinking, fever or sudden illness. Do not restart after a toxicity interruption until the team advises.

questions.q: Why do I need blood tests if I take tablets at home?
questions.a: Blood counts, kidney and liver results, together with symptoms, guide whether to continue and at what dose.

questions.q: Do I need a port or a pump?
questions.a: No take-home chemotherapy pump is used. Capecitabine is swallowed, so a central line is not required just to give it.

questions.q: What happens after treatment?
questions.a: Ask for your review and follow-up plan. Continue reporting symptoms after the last dose; further therapy depends on the treatment aim and response.

questions.q: Which checks continue when treatment changes or finishes?
questions.a: Keep reviewing bowel, bladder, skin, fatigue and nutrition effects during and after the course. Late effects and surgical assessment follow the radiation/colorectal team plan. Do not automatically extend tablets to make up missed radiation days or continue beyond the planned course.

evidence.title: Why this treatment is offered
evidence.intro: Capecitabine was an effective oral alternative to infused fluorouracil when combined with radiotherapy in the study. Outcomes included the whole treatment programme, including surgery.
evidence.interpretation: Capecitabine was an effective oral alternative to infused fluorouracil when combined with radiotherapy in the study. Outcomes included the whole treatment programme, including surgery.
evidence.population: 1,608 stage II/III rectal cancer patients receiving preoperative chemoradiation, then surgery.
evidence.limitations: Results concern the full multimodality programme; trial schedule changed during recruitment. No isolated tablet-course survival benefit can be inferred.
